title: Arena AI CEO says enterprises don’t know which AI models to trust
excerpt: Arena CEO Anastasios Angelopoulos said companies are "terrified" of working with frontier AI companies and China-based open models.
content_html:
By Brent D. Griffiths

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

Companies don't know which side to choose in AI, the leader of one of the largest model evaluators said.

"It's not only true that they're terrified of working with the frontier labs, but they're also terrified of working with the Chinese open source," Arena CEO Anastasios Angelopoulos said during a recent episode of the "20VC" podcast.

Angelopoulos said the companies he talks to are struggling to figure out where to build their AI future.

"I think we're in a really tricky situation for enterprises because just the way that the cards have landed," Angelopoulos told Business Insider during an interview where he expanded on his comments.

The current situation is, by all accounts, a bit messy. Arena has an up-close view. The company offers a crowdsourced AI model battle royale that lets users pit generative AI models against each other and vote on which one best completes the task. In September, it announced a commercial business where it would sell AI companies and businesses data gathered from the battles. In June, Arena announced it had reached $100 million in annualized run-rate revenue within 8 months of launching its enterprise service.

Frontier AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, offer cutting-edge models, but that technology can come with a steep price tag. The Trump administration's recent actions also illustrate that the model providers can be forced to shut off access without warning. Those companies, as Anthropic has demonstrated, can also impose safeguards on the models, which may mean that many companies cannot access the full extent of the model's capabilities.

"Anthropic or OpenAI could decide to turn off their AI at any moment if they feel that it is, quote unquote, 'unsafe,'" Angelopoulos told Business Insider. "And so if you're a business, what are you supposed to do? You want to be able to build on a stable and reliable AI stack."

In contrast, China-based open model companies, including Moonshot and DeepSeek, offer open-weight models that can be run locally, often at a fraction of the cost of frontier models. Some are worried about the security risks of relying on Chinese companies. Last month, Axios reported that the Trump administration has considered imposing restrictions or even issuing de facto bans on Chinese models.

Angelopoulos isn't the only one to hit on these themes. Palantir CEO Alex Karp has repeatedly warned that frontier AI companies, with which Palantir works, want to gather valuable intellectual property and data that they could then use to compete with their current customers.

"They deserve to colonize your enterprise," Karp said during Palantir's second-quarter earnings call on Monday, characterizing what he believed was the labs' attitude.

Palantir and Karp also have some incentive to stoke those fears, as the company offers its customers an application layer that allows businesses to control their data and the AI models they use.

Angelopoulos said Arena has experienced its own struggles with AI companies. He said that Arena has seen model providers use Arena's internal data "to serve synthetic battles and arenas to our employees in an effort to essentially get them to label data." Angelopoulos declined to name the offending companies, but said the practice "is not uncommon."

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company does business with frontier model makers and offers open models, has tried to strike a balance in the debate. He has said that companies will deploy both open models and proprietary ones, routing tasks based on both cost effectiveness and maintaining their IP.

"The world is going to have closed and open models," Huang recently told Axios. "We should use closed models as often as we can, and we should customize and use open models to build our own personal, our own customized AI if we must."

安杰洛普洛斯在接受《商业内幕》采访时详细阐述了自己的评论，他表示：“我认为，对于企业来说，我们正处于一个非常棘手的境地，因为卡片的落地方式就是如此。”

从各方面来看，目前的情况有点混乱。 竞技场可以近距离观看。 该公司提供了一种众包人工智能模型大逃杀，让用户可以让生成式人工智能模型相互竞争，并投票选出最能完成任务的模型。 9月，它宣布了一项商业业务，将出售从战斗中收集的人工智能公司和企业数据。 6 月，Arena 宣布推出企业服务后 8 个月内年化运行收入达到 1 亿美元。

包括 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 在内的前沿人工智能公司提供尖端模型，但该技术的价格可能很高。 特朗普政府最近的行动也表明，模型提供商可能会在没有警告的情况下被迫关闭访问。 正如 Anthropic 所证明的那样，这些公司还可以对模型施加保护措施，这可能意味着许多公司无法充分利用该模型的功能。

安哲罗普洛斯告诉《商业内幕》：“如果 Anthropic 或 OpenAI 觉得人工智能‘不安全’，他们可以随时决定关闭人工智能。” “那么如果你是一家企业，你应该做什么？ 你希望能够构建一个稳定可靠的人工智能堆栈。”

相比之下，包括Moonshot和DeepSeek在内的中国开放模型公司提供可以在本地运行的开放权重模型，而成本通常只是前沿模型的一小部分。 一些人担心依赖中国公司的安全风险。 上个月，Axios 报道称，特朗普政府已考虑对中国车型实施限制，甚至发布事实上的禁令。

安哲罗普洛斯并不是唯一一个触及这些主题的人。 Palantir 首席执行官亚历克斯·卡普 (Alex Karp) 多次警告，与 Palantir 合作的前沿人工智能公司希望收集有价值的知识产权和数据，然后用来与当前客户竞争。

卡普在周一 Palantir 第二季度财报电话会议上表示：“他们应该占领你的企业。”他描述了他认为实验室的态度。

Palantir 和 Karp 也有一些动机加剧这些担忧，因为该公司为客户提供了一个应用程序层，允许企业控制他们的数据和他们使用的人工智能模型。

安杰洛普洛斯表示，Arena 也经历过与人工智能公司的斗争。 他说，Arena 已经看到模型提供商使用 Arena 的内部数据“为我们的员工提供合成战斗和竞技场服务，以便从本质上让他们标记数据。” 安杰洛普洛斯拒绝透露违规公司的名称，但表示这种做法“并不罕见”。

英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋（Jensen Huang）的公司与前沿模型制造商有业务往来，并提供开放模型，他试图在争论中取得平衡。 他表示，公司将部署开放模型和专有模型，根据成本效益和维护 IP 来路由任务。

“世界将有封闭和开放的模式，”黄最近告诉 Axios。 “我们应该尽可能多地使用封闭模型，如果必须的话，我们应该定制和使用开放模型来构建我们自己的、我们自己定制的人工智能。”
